questions.q: A document sent by a seller to a prospective buyer showing the details, description, and prices of goods *before* the goods are actually ordered or dispatched is the...
questions.explain: A **Proforma Invoice** is a preliminary document sent to a buyer in advance of a shipment or delivery of goods. It provides an estimate of the costs, allowing the buyer to apply for an import license, foreign exchange, or simply to know what the final bill will look like.

questions.q: When a buyer returns damaged goods or is accidentally overcharged on an invoice, the seller will rectify the customer's account balance by issuing a...
questions.explain: A **Credit Note** is a commercial document issued by a seller to a buyer, reducing the amount that the buyer owes to the seller. It is used when goods are returned, there was a shortage in delivery, or the buyer was overcharged on the original invoice. (A *Debit Note* does the opposite—it increases the debt if the buyer was undercharged).

questions.q: An order placed by a home importer through an agent requesting the purchase of specific foreign goods from abroad is technically referred to as...
questions.explain: In foreign trade, an **Indent** is a formalized order sent by an importer to an exporter or buying agent abroad to purchase goods. An indent can be *open* (the agent chooses the manufacturer) or *closed* (the exact manufacturer is specified by the importer).

questions.q: Which of the following documents is specifically required by customs authorities to prove the specific country where imported goods were manufactured?
questions.explain: The **Certificate of Origin** is used in international trade to verify the exact nation in which goods were grown, produced, or manufactured. Customs officials use it to determine the correct import duties and to ensure goods are not coming from embargoed countries.

questions.q: The abbreviation **E & OE** (Errors and Omissions Excepted) is commonly printed at the bottom of an invoice to legally indicate that the seller...
options: guarantees the absolute accuracy of the invoice.
retains the right to correct any mathematical mistakes discovered later.
exempts the buyer from paying transport costs.
has successfully insured the goods against all transit risks.
questions.explain: **E & OE (Errors and Omissions Excepted)** protects the seller legally if there is an accidental error in the invoice (like a typo in pricing or missing an item). It gives the seller the right to amend the invoice after it has been sent.

questions.q: A manufacturer offers a $\text{Cash Discount}$ to a retailer primarily in order to...
options: enable the retailer to make a profit when reselling the goods.
compensate the retailer for buying goods in very large quantities.
encourage the prompt payment of outstanding debts.
cover the cost of transporting the goods to the retailer's warehouse.
questions.explain:
Different discounts serve different purposes:
*   **Cash Discount:** To encourage fast/prompt payment of debts.
*   **Trade Discount:** To enable the middleman (retailer) to make a profit off the catalog price (Option A).
*   **Quantity Discount:** To encourage bulk purchases (Option B).

questions.q: If a foreign supplier quotes a price as **CIF** (Cost, Insurance, and Freight), it implies that the quoted amount covers the cost of the goods plus...
options: insurance and transport charges up to the buyer's port of destination.
only the loading of goods onto the vessel at the seller's port.
the delivery of goods exactly to the buyer's inland warehouse.
insurance, freight, and the final import duties charged by the buyer's country.
questions.explain: **CIF (Cost, Insurance, and Freight)** means the seller pays for the goods, maritime insurance, and all shipping charges necessary to bring the goods to the named port of destination in the buyer's country. The buyer handles import duties and transport from the port to their own warehouse.

questions.q: Which of the following pricing terms means that the buyer is fully responsible for all costs and risks from the exact moment the goods leave the seller's factory gate?
questions.explain: **Ex-works (EXW)** is a trade term requiring the seller to make goods available at their own premises (factory or warehouse). The buyer must carry all costs, risks, and transport logistics from the seller's door to the final destination.

questions.q: A commercial arrangement where a customer immediately takes possession of an asset, but officially becomes the legal owner only after paying the final installment, is associated with...
questions.explain: While the syllabus broadly mentions "Purchase and deferred payment," a primary example is **Hire Purchase**. The buyer takes the goods immediately but pays for them in installments. Legal ownership remains with the seller until the very last installment is cleared.

questions.q: Bank notes and metal coins are exclusively accepted in a country's commercial transactions because they are...
options: backed by large reserves of gold in the central bank.
classified as legal tender by government legislation.
intrinsically more valuable than the metal they are made of.
immune to all forms of national inflation.
questions.explain: Bank notes and coins are **legal tender**. This means they are recognized by the law of the land as valid means of settling a public or private debt, and creditors are legally obligated to accept them.

questions.q: A businessman needs to make a large payment and wants to absolutely guarantee the payee that the funds are available and the instrument will not bounce. The most appropriate banking instrument to use is a...
questions.explain: A **Bank Draft** (or banker's cheque) is drawn by a bank on its own funds, not on an individual's account. Because the bank guarantees it, it is as good as cash and eliminates the risk of a bounced (dishonored) cheque.

questions.q: A customer who needs to pay a fixed subscription fee of $\text{₦}10,000$ automatically on the 5th day of every month to a specific organization would best utilize a...
questions.explain: A **Standing Order** is a written instruction from an account holder directing their bank to pay a specified, regular amount of money to another person or organization at predefined fixed intervals (e.g., monthly rent, subscriptions).

questions.q: The major difference between a bill of exchange and a promissory note is that...
options: a promissory note is an unconditional order to pay, while a bill of exchange is a promise.
a bill of exchange is drawn by the creditor, whereas a promissory note is drawn by the debtor.
a promissory note requires an endorsement by a commercial bank, whereas a bill does not.
a bill of exchange is issued by the post office, while a promissory note is issued by a bank.
questions.explain:
A **Bill of Exchange** is an unconditional *order* written by the person who is owed money (the creditor/drawer) addressed to the debtor. 
Conversely, a **Promissory Note** is an unconditional *promise* written by the person who owes the money (the debtor) pledging to pay the creditor.

questions.q: Which of the following represents the fastest and safest electronic method for remitting funds from an importer in Nigeria to an exporter located in Japan?
questions.explain: A **Telegraphic Transfer (TT)** or wire transfer is the fastest means of transferring money internationally. Banks use secure electronic networks (like SWIFT) to instantly move funds globally, making it far superior to mail transfers or money orders for foreign trade.
